body.text: A scorecard will not tell you what a company is worth. It will stop you from calling something a moat because you liked the story, and it will force you to write down what would change your mind.

children.text: Everything in Chapters 1 to 5 now folds into one sheet. The scorecard has twelve questions in three sections, each scored 0, 1, or 2, for a maximum of 24. The point is not the number. The point is that you cannot fill it in without doing the work, and once filled, it tells you exactly which parts of your thesis are weak.
Section A: Is There a Real Moat Source?
This section decides whether there is anything structural at all. Chapters 2, 3, and 4 supplied the tests.

cells: Can you name which of the five sources applies?
No clear source, only good execution
A clear source: intangibles, switching costs, network effects, cost advantage, or efficient scale
Do customers actually behave as if it exists?
Price increases stick, churn is low, or users concentrate on one platform
Is the advantage independent of one person, contract, or subsidy?
Depends on one promoter, client, or policy
Structural and independent of any single relationship
Would it survive the ₹10,000 crore test?
A well-funded rival could copy it in a few years
Money alone could not replicate it

body.text: Gating rule: if A1 or A4 scores zero, stop. The company cannot be a moat business regardless of how good the financials look, because excellent numbers with no structural reason are simply returns waiting to be competed away. Score the rest if you like, but cap your conclusion at "no moat".

children.text: Section B: Does the Financial Evidence Agree?
Chapter 5 supplied these. Use consolidated figures from Screener.in, adjusted for large cash balances where relevant.

cells: Minimum ROCE in the worst year
Operating margin range across the decade
Five-year cash conversion (operating cash ÷ net profit)

children.text: A moat is a claim about the future, so the final section is about direction and threats. Chapter 6 covers erosion in depth.

cells: Which way are returns and market share heading?
How exposed is it to regulatory or technology disruption?
High: a rule change or new technology could remove the advantage
Low: no visible threat over the next five years
Is there a runway to reinvest at these returns?
Long runway at high incremental returns

stats.label: 19 to 24
stats.context: Structural advantage with strong evidence and no visible threat

stats.label: 12 to 18
stats.context: Real but limited, or strong with a specific vulnerability

stats.label: 0 to 11
stats.context: A business, possibly a good one, without durable protection

body.text: The most valuable part of the scorecard is not the total. It is the list of criteria where you scored 0 or 1. Those are your thesis risks, written in your own words, and they are what you should re-check every time results are announced.

children.text: A hypothetical listed branded consumer company. Here is how the twelve scores came out.

cells: Brand with demonstrated pricing power, plus deep rural distribution
Raised prices in FY22 and FY23 with volumes still growing
No single customer, contract, or promoter dependency
A large rival could buy distribution and advertising, though not decades of trust
92% of profit converted to operating cash over five years
Quick commerce is shifting urban distribution
Low category penetration in smaller towns

body.title: Scorecard Totals by Section: Three Companies
Add Up the Scorecard
body.prompt: Using the worked example table above, what is the company's total score out of 24?
body.explanation: Section A = 7, Section B = 9, Section C = 4, giving 20 out of 24, or about 83%. That places it at the lower end of the wide moat band. The two scores of 1 in B5 and C2, incremental returns and quick commerce disruption, are exactly what this investor should track each quarter.

children.text: replace ROCE with ROE and return on assets, replace margin range with net interest margin stability, and add credit cost through a full cycle. Cash conversion is meaningless for lenders, so drop B4 and score out of 22.

judge B1 and B2 on the full-cycle average rather than the latest year, and add the company's position on the industry cost curve to A1. A low-cost producer in a cyclical industry can hold a narrow moat.
substitute take rate trend, contribution margin, and marketing spend as a percentage of revenue for B1 and B5 until reported returns become meaningful.
cap C3 at 1 where returns are regulated, since the regulator limits how much reinvestment can earn, and weight C2 heavily because tariff orders drive everything.

body.title: Apply the Gating Rule
body.question: A company scores 2 on every financial criterion in Section B and 2 on all of Section C, but you cannot identify any of the five moat sources, so A1 scores 0. What is the correct conclusion?
options: A wide moat, because the financial evidence is overwhelming
No moat: excellent numbers with no structural explanation are returns waiting to be competed away
A narrow moat, splitting the difference
Ignore the scorecard and buy on the numbers
body.explanation: This is the gating rule. Financial evidence describes what has happened; a moat source explains why it should continue. Without a source, high returns are most likely a good industry period, good execution, or luck, and none of those survive a determined competitor.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: The most useful output of the scorecard is not the total but the list of criteria scoring 0 or 1, because those are your thesis ___.
body.explanation: Low-scoring criteria tell you precisely what to monitor and what would prove your thesis wrong.

body.title: Two Scorecards, One Portfolio Decision
body.scenario: You score two companies. Company M, a listed exchange business, scores A: 8, B: 9, C: 3, total 20, with the C score dragged down by a pending regulatory consultation that could open its market. Company N, a branded apparel retailer, scores A: 5, B: 7, C: 5, total 17, with no regulatory threat but a weaker moat source, since A4 scored 1 and A1 scored 2 on brand alone. Both trade at similar valuations of about 45 times earnings.
body.prompt: What do the two scorecards tell you, and what should you do differently with each?
body.modelAnswer: Company M has the stronger moat today: a clear structural source with excellent financial evidence. But its weakness is concentrated in a single binary risk, a regulatory decision that could remove much of the advantage at once, as happened to power exchange investors. That means position sizing and a clear monitoring trigger matter more than further analysis: follow the consultation, and decide in advance what you will do under each outcome. Company N has no cliff-edge risk, but its moat is thinner and depends on a brand in a category where tastes shift and rivals can spend. Its risk is gradual erosion rather than a sudden shock, which shows up slowly in gross margins, same-store sales, and discounting. At 45 times earnings, both are priced as if their moats are secure, which suits neither profile perfectly. Practically: for M, size the position for the possibility of a bad regulatory outcome and watch one specific event; for N, watch quarterly margins and discounting, and accept that its moat deserves a lower multiple than M's if both are intact.

body.label: Use it twice
body.value: Score before you buy, and rescore once a year
body.context: A falling score, especially in Section C, is the earliest warning that a moat is narrowing.

body.title: Build Your Own Scorecard
steps: Copy the twelve criteria into a spreadsheet with columns for score and reason
Pick one company you already own and gather ten years of ROCE, margins, and cash flow from Screener.in
Score Section A first and apply the gating rule before going further
Score Sections B and C, writing one line of evidence for every score, not just the number
Total the score and place the company in the wide, narrow, or no moat band
List every criterion scoring 0 or 1 as your watch list for the next four quarters
Repeat for two competitors, so the score is comparative rather than absolute

body.text: The scorecard is an analytical discipline, not a valuation tool or a recommendation. Thresholds are deliberately rough and should be adjusted for the industry. All companies in this lesson are hypothetical.

points: The scorecard has twelve criteria in three sections, scored 0 to 2, for a maximum of 24 points
Section A tests the moat source, Section B the financial evidence, and Section C durability
The gating rule matters most: no identifiable source, or failing the ₹10,000 crore test, means no moat regardless of the numbers
Bands are 19 to 24 for wide, 12 to 18 for narrow, and 0 to 11 for none
Criteria scoring 0 or 1 are your thesis risks and your quarterly watch list
Adjust the criteria by industry: ROE for lenders, full-cycle averages for commodities, and unit economics for platforms
